title: The light fades
hook: Anuruddha and his friends lose their inner light; doubt, inattention, fear and more

segments.voice: Yesterday: tila, gravel and sesame, and your line, oil from sesame. Did you check what was really in the tub? Today, three old friends we've met before, and a light that keeps going out. Day four hundred ninety-six.

The hundred and twenty-eighth discourse opens with the Kosambi quarrel, the monks stabbing each other with words. The Buddha tries to make peace, and leaves. He walks alone, and eventually reaches a bamboo park where three monks live: Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila, the ones who live together like milk and water. They tell him how it is: whoever comes back first sets out the seats; whoever sees the water pot empty fills it. Then Anuruddha admits a problem. When we meditate, he says, a light appears, and visions. Then it fades, and we don't know why. Today: the light fades.
screen: `THE QUARREL AT KOSAMBI.` → `THREE FRIENDS, LIKE MILK AND WATER.` → `A LIGHT THAT FADES.`

segments.voice: The Buddha doesn't say the light was nothing. He says: I had this too, before my awakening. I saw light and forms, and they faded, and I had to find out why. Then he lists what he found, the imperfections of the mind, upakkilesa, one at a time. Doubt arose, and the light went. Inattention, and it went. Sleepiness and dullness. Fear, like a traveler who suddenly sees killers jump out on both sides of the road. Elation, like someone looking for one way into a hidden treasure who suddenly finds five. Inertia in the body. Then two about effort. Too much energy, like gripping a quail too tightly in your hand: it dies. Too little energy, like holding the quail too loosely: it flies away. Then longing. Then seeing too many different things. Then staring too hard at forms. Eleven in all. Each time, the Buddha says, he understood: this imperfection arose, and because of it my stillness fell away, and the light faded. And each time he resolved: I won't let that arise again. Today's discourse isn't telling anyone to chase lights. It's teaching that when something good fades, there's usually a reason, and the reason can be named. A quail held just right. Effort balanced like a hand that neither crushes nor drops.
screen: `I HAD THIS TOO` · `DOUBT, INATTENTION, FEAR` · `THE QUAIL: TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE` · `NAME IT, AND IT CAN BE LEFT` · then, large: `THE LIGHT FADES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing that dims you. Sit and settle. Think back over the last day or two to a moment when you felt clear or bright, and then it went. What came in just before? Doubt? Hurry? Too much effort, gripping the quail? Too little, letting it fly? Name it quietly, without blame. Then let the breath be held the way the quail should be: not crushed, not dropped. The bell holds the time.
Upakkilesa. Imperfections of the mind: the Buddha tells Anuruddha the inner light fades because of them, like doubt, fear and effort held too tight or too loose, and each can be named. Today's word.
Your line: a quail held just right. Today, when a good mood slips away, ask what came in just before it, and name that one thing. Day four hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Some meditation teachers use the quail simile from MN 128 to describe balanced effort, and students in several traditions learn to notice and name hindrances such as doubt and dullness when concentration falls away.

myth: the Buddha tells Anuruddha the light was imaginary
he says he had it too before his awakening, and teaches why it fades.
from doubt and inattention to effort too tight or too loose and staring too hard at forms.
the three friends quarrel at the start of MN 128
the quarrel is among the monks at Kosambi; Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila live in harmony.

fork.setup: you're holding a quail in your hand. how should you hold it, in the Buddha's picture of effort?
options: neither too tight nor too loose.
fork.reveal: too tight and it dies; too loose and it flies away. balanced effort is the hand that holds it just right.

original.note: Pali upakkilesa: imperfection, a defilement of the mind. the title of MN 128.

trapdoor: what you thought: if a good feeling in meditation fades, you did something wrong.
what it means: it fades for reasons, doubt, fear, effort too tight or too loose, and each can be named.
what a scholar hears: MN 128 joins the Kosambi narrative to an autobiographical account of the Buddha's own pre-awakening practice with light (obhasa) and forms.

notes: MN 128 paraphrased. Confirm the eleven imperfections and their order: doubt, inattention, sloth and torpor, fear, elation, inertia, excess energy, deficient energy, longing, perception of diversity, excessive meditation on forms.
Confirm the similes: travelers with murderers, one treasure finding five, quail gripped too tightly / too loosely.
Callbacks to day 427 (milk and water, MN 31) and day 440 (the Kosambi quarrel, MN 48).
